title: Debt & Credit
description: Use debt as a tool, not a leash.
wolfLine: Interest works against you too. Fight back.

debt.definition: Money you've borrowed and still have to pay back.
debt.example: You borrow $1,000 from a bank. You now have $1,000 of debt.

loan.definition: Money a lender gives you now, which you repay over time, usually with interest.
loan.example: A car loan: the bank pays for the car, you pay the bank back each month.

credit-card.definition: A card that lets you buy now and pay later. Whatever you don't pay off each month gets charged interest.
credit-card.example: Buy a $500 TV on the card, pay $100 this month, and you're charged interest on the other $400.

good-debt.definition: Cheap borrowing for something that builds your future, like a home or a skill that raises your pay.
good-debt.example: An affordable loan for training that gets you a better-paid job.

bad-debt.definition: Expensive borrowing for things that quickly lose their value.
bad-debt.example: A holiday paid for on a credit card you can't pay off.

mortgage.definition: A big loan used to buy a home, usually paid back over 15 to 30 years.
mortgage.example: The bank lends you most of the price of a flat, and you repay it monthly.

apr.definition: Annual Percentage Rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage. Higher means more expensive.
apr.example: Borrow $1,000 at 10% APR for a year and it costs you about $100.

balance.definition: How much you still owe on a card or loan right now.
balance.example: Spend $700 on a card, pay back $200, and your balance is $500.

minimum-payment.definition: The smallest amount a lender lets you pay each month. Pay only this and your debt shrinks very slowly.
minimum-payment.example: You owe $2,000, but the card only asks for $40 this month.

avalanche-method.definition: A way to pay off debts: pay the minimum on all of them, then put every spare bit of money toward the one with the highest APR.
avalanche-method.example: Clear the 29% store card before the 7% car loan.

snowball-method.definition: A way to pay off debts: pay the minimum on all of them, then attack the smallest balance first for quick wins.
snowball-method.example: Clear the $400 phone plan before the $7,500 car loan.

credit-score.definition: A number that tells lenders how reliable you are at paying back money. Higher is better.
credit-score.example: A good score can get you a loan with a lower APR.

credit-limit.definition: The most you're allowed to borrow on a credit card.
credit-limit.example: A card with a $2,000 limit lets you owe up to $2,000 on it.

credit-utilization.definition: How much of your credit limit you're using, as a percentage: balance ÷ limit. Lower is better for your credit score.
credit-utilization.example: Owe $500 on a $1,000 limit and your utilization is 50%.

lessons.title: What Is Debt?
lessons.summary: Borrowing, loans, and what it really costs.

steps.context: [[Debt]] is money you've borrowed and still have to pay back.
steps.prompt: You borrow $1,000 from a bank to buy a laptop. What do you now have?
steps.explain: Borrowed money isn't yours to keep. It's debt until you pay it back.

steps.context: A [[loan]] is one common way to borrow: a lender gives you money now, and you pay it back over time. You usually pay back **more** than you borrowed. The extra is [[interest]], and this time you're the one paying it.
steps.prompt: You borrow $1,000 and pay back $1,100 in total. What's the extra $100?
steps.explain: The price of using someone else's money.

steps.context: A [[credit card]] lets you buy now and pay later. If you don't pay the full bill each month, you're charged interest on what's left, and it's usually a lot.
steps.prompt: You buy a $500 TV on a credit card and pay back $100 this month. What happens to the other $400?
steps.explain: Whatever you don't pay off keeps costing you.

steps.context: Cheap borrowing that builds your future, like a home or a skill that raises your pay, is often called [[good debt]]. Expensive borrowing for things that quickly lose value is [[bad debt]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is closest to bad debt?
choices: A low-cost loan for training that raises your pay
A holiday on a credit card you can't pay off
An affordable loan to buy a home
steps.explain: High interest, and the holiday is over long before the debt is.

steps.prompt: All debt is bad.
steps.explain: Cheap debt that builds your future can be a smart move. Expensive debt for fun rarely is.

steps.context: A [[mortgage]] is a big loan used to buy a home. People usually pay it back over 15 to 30 years.
steps.prompt: What is a mortgage for?
steps.explain: Homes cost too much to buy outright, so most people borrow.

steps.prompt: Recap: match each word to what it means.
pairs: Borrowed money you repay over time
A loan to buy a home
The extra you pay to borrow

lessons.title: APR, Decoded
lessons.summary: What borrowing really costs you each year.

steps.context: Lenders show the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage called the [[APR]]. A higher APR means more expensive debt.
steps.prompt: One card has a 12% APR. Another has 24%. Which is cheaper to borrow on?
steps.explain: Lower APR, lower cost.

steps.context: Rough yearly cost = amount you owe × APR. Owe $1,000 at 10% APR for a year and it costs about $1,000 × 0.10 = $100.
steps.prompt: You owe $2,000 on a card at 20% APR for a whole year. Roughly how much interest is that?
steps.explain: $2,000 × 0.20 = $400. Cards add interest monthly, so the real number is a bit higher.

steps.context: The amount you still owe on a card or loan is your [[balance]].
steps.prompt: You spent $700 on your card and paid back $200. What's your balance?

steps.context: Every month, a card asks for at least a small [[minimum payment]]. Pay only that, and interest keeps the balance alive for a very long time.
steps.prompt: What happens if you only ever pay the minimum?
choices: The debt is gone in a month
The card company forgives the rest
The debt drags on for years because of interest
steps.explain: Minimums are designed to keep you paying. Pay more whenever you can.

steps.context: Stretching a loan over more years makes each monthly payment smaller, but you pay interest for longer.
steps.prompt: A smaller monthly payment always means a cheaper loan.
steps.explain: Smaller payments over more years can cost more in total.

steps.prompt: APR stands for Annual Percentage ___.
steps.explain: Annual Percentage Rate.

lessons.title: Avalanche vs. Snowball
lessons.summary: Two ways to kill debt. Pick your weapon.

steps.context: The [[avalanche method]]: pay the minimum on every debt, then put every spare bit of money toward the one with the **highest APR**.
steps.prompt: Using the avalanche method, which debt do you attack first?
steps.explain: Highest APR first. It's costing you the most.

steps.prompt: Avalanche method: order these debts from first to last to pay off.
steps.explain: Highest APR to lowest.

steps.context: The [[snowball method]]: pay the minimum on everything, then attack the **smallest balance** first. Every debt you clear feels like a win.
steps.prompt: Using the snowball method, which debt goes first?
steps.explain: Smallest balance first. Quick win, then roll that money into the next one.

steps.prompt: Snowball method: order these debts from first to last to pay off.
steps.explain: Smallest balance to biggest.

steps.prompt: Which method usually saves the most money overall?
steps.explain: Clearing the highest APR first means less interest. Snowball wins on motivation.

steps.prompt: With either method, you keep paying the minimum on every debt.
steps.explain: Missed minimums mean fees and damage. Extra money goes to one target.

lessons.title: Credit Scores
lessons.summary: The reputation lenders check before they say yes.

steps.context: Your [[credit score]] is a number that tells lenders how reliable you are at paying back money. Higher is better.
steps.prompt: What does a high credit score usually get you?
choices: Easier approval and a lower APR
steps.explain: Lenders charge less to people they trust.

steps.prompt: Which habit helps your credit score most?
choices: Opening lots of cards at once
Missing a payment now and then
steps.explain: On-time payments are the biggest single factor. Never miss.

steps.context: Your [[credit limit]] is the most you're allowed to borrow on a card.
steps.prompt: Your card has a $5,000 credit limit. What does that mean?
choices: You can owe up to $5,000 on it
steps.explain: It's a ceiling, not a target.

steps.context: [[Credit utilization]] is how much of your limit you're using: balance ÷ limit, as a percentage. Owe $500 on a $1,000 limit and you're at 50%.
steps.prompt: Your limit is $5,000 and your balance is $1,500. What's your utilization?
Lower credit utilization is generally better for your credit score.
steps.explain: Using a small slice of your limit shows you're not stretched.

steps.prompt: Checking your own credit score lowers it.
steps.explain: Looking at your own score is free and harmless.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you're closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Debt
lessons.summary: Eight questions. Three strikes and you're out.

steps.prompt: You only ever pay the minimum on a credit card. What happens?
choices: The balance clears within a year
Interest keeps the debt alive for years
Your credit limit drops to zero
steps.explain: Pay above the [[minimum payment]] whenever you can.

steps.prompt: Avalanche method: order from first to last to pay off.
steps.explain: Highest APR first.

steps.prompt: A $3,000 balance sits at 18% APR for a year. Roughly how much interest is that?
The snowball method pays off the highest APR first.
steps.explain: That's the avalanche. Snowball goes smallest balance first.

steps.prompt: The yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage, is the ___.
steps.explain: Annual Percentage Rate.
